title: To You I Call, O My Rock
summary: The psalmist begs God not to be silent, fearing that without an answer he will be like those going down to the Pit. Lifting his hands toward the sanctuary, he asks not to be dragged away with the wicked, who speak peace while planning harm, and asks God to repay them for their deeds. Then his prayer turns to praise: God has heard. The LORD is his strength and shield, and the psalm ends with a prayer for God to save, bless, shepherd, and carry his people forever.
story: Psalm 28 closes the small group of psalms (26 to 28) that center on the sanctuary. Like Psalm 26, it asks not to be swept away with the wicked; like Psalm 27, it fears God's silence and ends with confidence. It moves the whole way from lament to thanksgiving in nine verses, a movement found in many psalms, and it ends by widening from the individual to the king and the whole people, as Psalm 25 did. It prepares for Psalm 29, where the voice of the LORD that the psalmist longed to hear thunders over the waters.
historical:
The heading reads Of David. Traditional readers take it as David's prayer, perhaps during a time of illness or danger, and the reference to the LORD's anointed in verse 8 fits a king praying for himself in the third person or a worshiper praying for the king. Many modern scholars read of David as a collection heading and see the psalm as a lament used at the temple, of uncertain date. The inner sanctuary in verse 2 suggests the temple of Solomon or the tabernacle before it.

Some interpreters think the sudden shift in verse 6 reflects an event in worship: a priest or prophet may have spoken a word of assurance after verse 5, and the psalmist responded with praise. Others think the psalmist simply moved, within his own prayer, from pleading to confidence. The text records the turn but not its cause.
cultural:
The Pit (bor) was a word for a cistern or dungeon, and in poetry it became a name for the grave and the realm of the dead, often paired with Sheol. To go down to the Pit was to die, and for an Israelite it meant being cut off from the worship of God in the land of the living (Psalm 88:4-5). God's silence felt like the first step toward it.

Lifting hands toward the sanctuary was a common posture of prayer in the ancient Near East, with palms raised and open. Verse 2 specifies the inner sanctuary (devir), the innermost room of the temple where the ark stood (1 Kings 6:19). Israelites who could not enter it, and those far from Jerusalem, turned toward it in prayer, as Solomon's dedication prayer invites (1 Kings 8:29-30). The picture of the wicked speaking peace (shalom) to neighbors while malice fills their hearts describes flattery and betrayal within the community, sins the Psalms and Proverbs condemn repeatedly.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament with a turn to thanksgiving. Verses 1 to 5 are plea and petition, including a request for judgment on the wicked. Verse 6 is the hinge, beginning with blessed be the LORD and repeating the very words of verse 2: he has heard my cry for mercy. Verses 6 and 7 give thanks, and verses 8 and 9 widen the scope to the anointed king and the people. The word works or deeds recurs deliberately: God is asked to repay the wicked for the works of their hands (verse 4), because they pay no regard to the works of the LORD and what his hands have done (verse 5). The final verse gathers four verbs (save, bless, shepherd, carry), a compact summary of what God does for his people.

outline.t: Be not silent: a cry toward the sanctuary
Do not drag me away with the wicked; repay them
Blessed be the LORD, who has heard
Strength for the anointed; save and shepherd your people

doctrines.note: The psalm shows prayer as a desperate need for God's answer, since his silence feels like death. It also shows prayer changing within itself, as the one who pleads comes to give thanks.
The psalmist asks God to repay the wicked according to their deeds, entrusting justice to God rather than taking it himself. The ground is that they disregard God's works.
The last verse prays for God's people as his inheritance, his flock to be shepherded and carried forever. Personal rescue ends in concern for the whole community.

words.note: Bor, pit, cistern, or dungeon. Joseph was thrown into a bor (Genesis 37:24), and Jeremiah into one (Jeremiah 38:6). In poetry it became a name for the grave and the world of the dead. The psalmist fears that God's silence will leave him among those going down to it.

Devir, the inner sanctuary, the innermost room of the temple, also called the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood beneath the cherubim (1 Kings 6:19-23). Lifting hands toward it meant turning toward the place of God's special presence among his people.

Nachalah, inheritance, an allotted portion passed down in a family. In Israel it usually referred to the family land. In verse 9 God's people are his inheritance, a remarkable reversal: not only is the land Israel's portion, but Israel is God's (Deuteronomy 32:9).

Mashiach, anointed. Israel's kings were anointed with oil to mark God's choice of them. In verse 8 God is the stronghold of salvation for his anointed, linking the individual's rescue with God's care for the king of David's line. The word is the source of Messiah.

christ: The psalm ends with a prayer for God to shepherd his people and carry them forever, and it links the people's salvation with God's anointed king. The New Testament presents Jesus as both the anointed king and the shepherd of God's people, who gathers the lost and carries them (Luke 15:4-5 pictures a shepherd carrying a found sheep on his shoulders). The psalm's fear of going down to the Pit also has an echo in Christ, who truly went down into death and whose resurrection means that the Pit is not the end for those who belong to him. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 28, so these are thematic connections. The psalm's movement from God's silence to he has heard is one Christians trace in Jesus' own prayers, heard because of his reverence (Hebrews 5:7).

hard.q: Is it right to ask God to repay people for the evil they have done, as verse 4 does?
hard.a: Prayers like verse 4 appear often in the Psalms and trouble many readers, especially in light of Jesus' command to pray for enemies. Several points help. The psalmist asks God, not himself, to act, handing over his desire for justice rather than taking revenge (compare Romans 12:19, which quotes Deuteronomy 32:35). He asks for justice in proportion to the deeds, not for cruelty. And the wicked here are those who destroy the community by deceit and have no regard for God's works. Some Christians read such prayers as appropriate cries for justice that the church can still pray against evil and oppression; others see them as honest expressions of pain that are brought to God and transformed there, especially in light of the cross, where Jesus prayed for his enemies' forgiveness. Most interpreters agree that the psalm does not permit personal vengeance.

questions: The psalmist fears God's silence more than anything. How have you experienced silence in prayer, and what did you do with it?
The wicked speak peace while plotting harm. Where are you tempted to say one thing while meaning another?
The psalm turns from pleading to thanksgiving. What prayer has God answered that you have not yet thanked him for?
